target: Nació mi sobrina el viernes.
english: My niece was born on Friday.
tip: 'Nació mi sobrina' puts the verb first – Spanish often places the subject after the verb when it's the new information. English keeps subject-first order.

target: Le peiné el pelo a mi hija.
english: I combed my daughter's hair.
tip: Combing someone else's hair? 'Le' claims ownership: 'le peiné el pelo' – the 'le' says it's my daughter's, so no 'su pelo' needed.

target: Me multaron por estacionar en doble fila.
english: I got fined for double parking.
tip: No passive needed: 'me multaron' = they fined me. Spanish uses an anonymous 'they' where English reaches for 'I got fined.'

target: Me quedé en blanco durante la presentación.
english: My mind went blank during the presentation.
tip: 'Me quedé en blanco' – I stayed in blank. Quedarse marks the state you end up in; here, going blank mid-presentation.

target: La reunión fue cancelada sin previo aviso.
english: The meeting was cancelled without prior notice.
tip: Passive participles agree like adjectives: 'la reunión fue cancelada' – cancelada, feminine, matching la reunión. 'Cancelado' would grate.

target: Me lavo la cara con agua fría.
english: I wash my face with cold water.
tip: With reflexive verbs and body parts, Spanish uses the definite article ("la cara"), not a possessive ("mi cara"). The reflexive "me" already tells you whose face.

target: Le echó una mano con las maletas.
english: He gave him a hand with the suitcases.
tip: 'Echó una mano' – threw a hand? Echar is Spanish's do-everything verb; echar una mano = lend a hand. You throw it, you don't lend it.

target: Mi padre siempre dice que hay que madrugar.
english: My father always says you have to get up early.
tip: Spanish has a single verb for getting up early: madrugar. 'Hay que madrugar' = you have to get up early – one word, no phrase needed.

target: La aduana nos hizo abrir todas las maletas.
english: Customs made us open all the suitcases.
tip: 'La aduana nos hizo abrir' – hacer + infinitive = make someone do something. The person forced to act appears as a pronoun ('nos') before hacer.

target: Él se puso contento al oír la noticia.
english: He became happy when he heard the news.
tip: English 'became' is one verb; Spanish picks by type. 'Se puso contento' – ponerse is for quick, temporary mood shifts, not lasting change.

target: Hacía mucho calor y las ventanas estaban abiertas.
english: It was very hot and the windows were open.
tip: Imperfect for background descriptions: hacía calor, estaban abiertas.

target: El momento en que supe la verdad cambió todo.
english: The moment I found out the truth, everything changed.
tip: Saber in the preterite isn't 'knew' – it's found out. 'Supe la verdad' = the moment the truth hit me. Ongoing knowledge would be sabía.

target: Fue tal la impresión que nos causó que decidimos quedarnos una semana más.
english: The impression it made on us was so strong that we decided to stay another week.
tip: "Tal... que" (such... that) – consecutive construction expressing result/consequence.

target: Antes no existían los celulares.
english: Before, cellphones didn't exist.
tip: Things in general take the article: 'los celulares' = cellphones as a category. English drops 'the' for generalizations; Spanish never does.

target: Me tocó organizar el evento de empresa.
english: I had to organize the company event.
tip: 'Me tocó organizar' – literally 'it touched me to organize.' Tocar means the task fell to you by luck or duty, not by choice.

target: Llueve sobre mojado; ya teníamos bastantes problemas.
english: When it rains, it pours; we already had enough problems.
tip: Llover sobre mojado = when bad things pile up on existing problems.

target: La entrevista fue muy bien.
english: The interview went very well.
tip: This 'fue' isn't ser – it's IR: the interview WENT very well. Ser and ir share the same preterite (fui, fue), so only context tells you was vs went.

target: Una copa de vino tinto.
english: A glass of red wine.
tip: Wine is ordered by the 'copa' – the stemmed glass – and just 'una copa' on its own implies alcohol. A vaso is a plain tumbler; 'vaso de vino' sounds rustic.

target: Quiero la carta, por favor.
english: I want the menu, please.
tip: "La carta" is the menu in a restaurant. "El menú" often refers to a fixed-price meal (menú del día).

target: De pequeño, yo leía mucho.
english: As a child, I read a lot.
tip: 'De pequeño' = literally 'of small' = when I was little. De + adjective is Spanish's shortcut for 'as a child' – no when-I-was clause needed.

target: Me preguntó si tenía hambre.
english: She asked me if I was hungry.
tip: Hunger is something you HAVE, not something you ARE: 'tenía hambre' = I had hunger. Same with thirst, fear, sleep – tener, never estar.

target: Él tuvo un accidente de carro.
english: He had a car accident.
tip: 'Carro' = car in Latin America; in Spain a carro is a horse-drawn cart and cars are coches. Say carro in Mexico, coche in Madrid.

target: Por aquí hay muchos restaurantes buenos.
english: Around here there are many good restaurants.
tip: "Por aquí" = around here / this way. "Por" for approximate location or direction.

target: Mi tía vivía sola desde hacía años.
english: My aunt had been living alone for years.
tip: English needs 'had been living'; Spanish keeps plain imperfect + desde hacía: 'vivía sola desde hacía años' = she lived alone since it-made years.

target: Ya sabía la noticia cuando me llamaste.
english: I already knew the news when you called me.
tip: "Ya" + imperfect (sabía) for prior state + preterite (llamaste) for the moment of calling.

target: Se me fue el santo al cielo y olvide la cita.
english: My mind went completely blank and I forgot the appointment.
tip: Literally 'the saint went off to heaven on me' – the standard idiom for your mind going blank mid-thought. That's why it leads straight to forgetting la cita.

target: ¿A qué hora cierra la catedral?
english: What time does the cathedral close?
tip: Questions flip the order: verb first, subject after. 'Cierra la catedral' = closes the cathedral. There's no 'does' helper – the flip IS the question.

target: Trabajo para una empresa de tecnología.
english: I work for a tech company.
tip: "Para" = for (employer): "Trabajo para Google." Para for who you work for.

target: Reservé la habitación para tres noches.
english: I booked the room for three nights.
tip: "Para" indicates purpose/destination. "For three nights" = the intended duration of the stay.

target: Cuando empecé, no sabía usar la impresora.
english: When I started, I didn't know how to use the printer.
tip: No 'how to' needed: saber + infinitive already means knowing HOW. 'No sabía usar la impresora' = I didn't know to-use the printer. Adding cómo sounds English.
